problem: End-to-end imitation-learning navigation policies (ViNT, NoMaD) supervise the vision encoder only indirectly through the action loss, so it learns action-agnostic features and gives inconsistent actions at ambiguous decision points such as intersections. Prior control-oriented neural-collapse pretraining assumes a Simplex ETF geometry with equidistant categorical classes, which does not fit ordered goal-relative directions.
motivation: Goal-relative steering classes from Far Left to Far Right are naturally ordinal, since neighboring classes share visual context and opposing ones differ. Ordinal neural collapse theory says such classes collapse onto a 1D ordered subspace rather than a simplex. Imposing this geometry on the encoder should give control-relevant, consistent representations, which matters most in visually ambiguous multi-way intersections.
key_idea: Pretrain the navigation vision encoder so goal-relative direction classes align along a single supervised ordinal axis with off-axis variance suppressed, then fine-tune the full NoMaD diffusion pipeline end-to-end.
insight: A geometry matched to the task matters: NC-ETF pretraining with the wrong (simplex) geometry is comparable to or worse than NoMaD, and CE-only direction supervision is actively harmful (16% SR vs 48% NoMaD on Multi-Intersection). All three loss terms contribute (CDNV only 33 → +ord 45 → full 74 SR). The pretraining must be staged: joint training with the ORION losses collapses to 0% SR, and the ordinal structure from Stage 1 persists after Stage 2 (Far–Near mode separation 6–9× larger than NoMaD).
method: Goal-relative control classes: the angular offset between heading and goal is split into K=5 uniform bins over the front [-90°,90°] (ordered Far Right to Far Left) plus one out-of-view class, giving 6 classes; the out-of-view class is used only in the CDNV loss.
CDNV class separability loss: minimizes within-class variance relative to squared distance between centered class means over all class pairs.

Supervised ordinal projection: the axis w is the normalized sum of centered class means weighted by equally spaced targets t_k = k-(K-1)/2; L_ord is the MSE between projected class means and targets, which enforces class ordering by construction.
Orthogonal compactness: L_orth penalizes within-class feature variance in the subspace orthogonal to w, pushing features toward the 1D ordinal axis.
Stable statistics: running class means and variances via Welford's algorithm, EMA smoothing of w, and losses computed from current-batch features centered with the updated statistics.

Two-stage training: Stage 1 pretrains only the EfficientNet-B0 encoder features h_t (not context z_t) for 30 epochs with all lambdas = 1; Stage 2 fine-tunes encoder, Transformer context and diffusion decoder end-to-end with NoMaD's loss for 30 epochs.

setting.backbone: NoMaD architecture: EfficientNet-B0 encoder + Transformer context + 1D conditional U-Net diffusion decoder (trained; encoder pretrained with ORION losses)
setting.training_data: NoMaD dataset (RECON, SCAND, GoStanford, SACSoN; ~140 h), goal images sampled 3-20 steps ahead, with direction-class labels derived from the goal-relative angle
setting.observation: monocular RGB current/past frames plus goal image (ZED 2i left RGB on the real robot)
setting.action_space: continuous waypoint trajectories from diffusion decoder (horizon 8)
setting.simulator: Stanford 2D-3D-S (indoor) and Gazebo Citysim (outdoor); real robot Clearpath Husky
setting.privileged: none at test time (direction labels used only for pretraining; topological visual subgoals as in NoMaD)

numbers.extra: Sim, Husky UGV; 1.0 m success tolerance, 300 s limit

numbers.eval_set_note: 100 trials, ~200 m route, four directional decisions

numbers.extra: Real Husky UGV, ZED 2i, Jetson Orin

numbers_note: All benchmarks are the authors' own custom simulated/real routes, not standard public benchmarks; the 'test' split label is a placeholder. Ablation variants (CE-only, NC-Joint, loss ablations) exist in Tables 3-4 but are not listed here.
results: ORION beats NoMaD on every simulated route, e.g. Citysim Multi-Intersection SR 74 vs 48 (+26 pp) and Indoor Intersection SR 91 vs 17. Heading jerk falls 71% on Multi-Intersection (34.49 → 10.13). In the real world it improves SR to 60/70/33.33 vs NoMaD 40/60/16.67 on Indoor/Campus/Field, and outperforms NC-ETF and ViNT.
limitations: Evaluation uses few trials in the real world (6-10 per route) and custom routes, so statistical power is limited and there are no public benchmarks.
Requires direction-labeled pretraining data and a hand-designed discretization (K=5 plus an out-of-view class); bin-boundary label ambiguity remains.
Branch misjudgment and premature turning failures persist, and Field success remains low (33%); H-Jerk is not always best (ViNT lower in some cases).
